PHASE 7 · FNP CERTIFICATION REVIEW & CLINICAL INTEGRATION

Week 157 — Lesson 181: Urgent & Emergency Clinical Integration Board Review

FNP-level goal: Rapidly identify unstable physiology, initiate care within training and setting capability, avoid delay from premature diagnostic closure, activate emergency resources, and complete a safe closed-loop handoff for time-critical illness or injury.

Learning Objectives

  • Use first impression and ABCDE assessment before pursuing a final diagnosis.
  • Recognize emergencies involving airway, breathing, circulation, neurologic function, trauma, toxic exposure, pregnancy, or behavioral safety.
  • Integrate vital-sign trends, medications, comorbidities, age, pregnancy possibility, function, and trajectory.
  • Recognize ACS, aortic disease, PE, stroke, sepsis, anaphylaxis, respiratory failure, metabolic crisis, hemorrhage, seizure, and poisoning.
  • Stabilize within scope while arranging EMS transport to an appropriate receiving level of care.
  • Avoid unsafe private transport, delayed referral, indiscriminate testing, and treatments that impede definitive care.
  • Communicate acuity, interventions, response, uncertainty, and pending risks through a structured handoff.
  • Close the loop after emergency disposition through documentation, result ownership, reconciliation, and follow-up.

Part 1 — The FIRST-AID Framework

  • F — First impression: appearance, position, speech, breathing effort, color, behavior, and obvious bleeding.
  • I — Immediate threats: airway obstruction, respiratory failure, shock, cardiac arrest, severe neurologic change, or hemorrhage.
  • R — Rapid ABCDE: airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure/environment.
  • S — Stabilize within capability: activate help, position safely, support oxygenation and ventilation as indicated, control bleeding, monitor, and use emergency protocols.
  • T — Time-critical differential: identify lethal diagnoses and the intervention or destination each requires.
  • A — Activate and assign: call EMS early, identify a leader, delegate tasks, and prepare equipment and records.
  • I — Information handoff: baseline, onset, findings, interventions, response, medications, allergies, and uncertainty.
  • D — Disposition and documentation: safest transport, receiving facility, transfer record, family communication, and follow-up ownership.

Part 2 — Stable vs Unstable

Do not define stability by blood pressure alone. Instability may be airway compromise, severe respiratory effort, hypoxemia, poor perfusion, altered mental status, ongoing ischemia, evolving neurologic deficit, uncontrolled bleeding, dangerous toxidrome, inability to maintain safety, or rapid deterioration.

A patient can remain temporarily normotensive while compensating for sepsis, hemorrhage, PE, or anaphylaxis. One abnormal vital sign may reflect pain or fear, but persistent abnormalities require explanation and reassessment.

Part 3 — Setting Capability Determines the Plan

A clinic, telehealth visit, urgent care, and emergency department have different personnel, monitoring, medications, imaging, and resuscitation capacity. A condition safely observed in one setting may require immediate transfer from another. Know the location of the AED, oxygen, rescue medication, emergency numbers, and staff roles before a crisis.

Do not delay EMS while attempting a workup the setting cannot complete or monitor. A normal office test cannot compensate for unavailable serial assessment or definitive treatment.

Part 4 — The First 60 Seconds

Look before taking a long history. Can the patient speak? Is there stridor, gasping, cyanosis, diaphoresis, pallor, uncontrolled bleeding, asymmetric weakness, seizure, or collapse? Determine responsiveness and whether normal breathing and circulation are present.

If cardiac arrest is suspected, activate emergency response, begin high-quality CPR, and apply an AED according to current AHA training and local protocol. Resuscitation is a psychomotor competency; written review does not replace current BLS, ACLS, or PALS preparation.

Part 5 — Airway

Threats include foreign body, anaphylaxis, angioedema, facial or neck trauma, burns, secretions, blood, reduced consciousness, and deep-neck infection. Stridor, gurgling, drooling, muffled voice, swelling, or inability to handle secretions demands rapid action.

Keep a patient with critical upper-airway obstruction calm, call airway-capable resources early, and avoid unnecessary examination that worsens obstruction. Becoming quiet can mean loss of airflow or consciousness—not improvement.

Part 6 — Breathing

Assess rate, depth, work, symmetry, air entry, breath sounds, saturation signal quality, speech, and fatigue. Cyanosis, apnea, severe retractions, silent chest, altered state, unilateral absent breath sounds with instability, or progressive exhaustion requires emergency support.

A normal saturation does not exclude hypercapnia, PE, severe work of breathing, or impending fatigue. Poor perfusion, movement, and device limitations can distort measurements.

Part 7 — Circulation

Assess pulse, rhythm, blood-pressure trend, capillary refill, skin, mental status, urine history, bleeding, and congestion. Ask whether the mechanism is low volume, pump failure, obstructed flow, vasodilation, or a mixture.

Control external hemorrhage immediately. Do not wait for hypotension: tachycardia, cool skin, confusion, oliguria, weak pulses, or narrowing pulse pressure may signal shock earlier.

Part 8 — Disability and Neurologic Assessment

Assess consciousness, orientation, speech, pupils, facial symmetry, arm drift, gross strength, and glucose. Determine last known well when stroke is possible and obtain collateral history.

Altered mental status is a syndrome. Consider hypoxia, hypoglycemia, stroke, seizure, infection, poison, metabolic disease, trauma, organ failure, temperature illness, withdrawal, and psychiatric causes. Do not label a physiologic emergency as behavioral prematurely.

Part 9 — Exposure, Environment, and Reassessment

Look for rash, trauma, bleeding, swelling, medication patches, injection sites, medical-alert devices, and exposure clues while protecting privacy and body temperature. Ask about pregnancy, immune status, anticoagulants, insulin, substances, and procedures.

Reassess ABCDE, symptoms, and vital signs after every meaningful action. Temporary improvement does not automatically make private transport safe; anaphylaxis, arrhythmia, neurologic deficit, severe asthma, hypoglycemia, and opioid toxicity can recur.

Part 10 — Chest Pain: Time-Critical Differential

Consider acute coronary syndrome, aortic dissection, PE, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, esophageal rupture, and other cardiopulmonary disease. Indigestion, dyspnea, fatigue, diaphoresis, nausea, or weakness may be an ischemic equivalent.

Assess onset, provocation, quality, radiation, associated symptoms, hemodynamics, examination, and ECG when immediately available. Reproducible pain or antacid response cannot independently exclude ACS.

Part 11 — Acute Coronary Syndrome

Ongoing concerning pressure, ischemic equivalents, instability, new arrhythmia, heart failure, or an ischemic ECG pattern requires EMS and emergency evaluation. A normal initial ECG or very early biomarker does not close the diagnosis.

Do not send a high-risk patient by private car because an office ECG is nondiagnostic. Use current protocols for immediate medications, checking allergy, bleeding, interaction, and aortic-dissection concerns.

Part 12 — Aortic Emergency

Sudden severe chest, back, or abdominal pain; pulse or blood-pressure asymmetry; neurologic deficit; syncope; new aortic regurgitation findings; or known aortic disease should raise concern. Presentation may mimic ACS, stroke, or abdominal disease.

Activate EMS and communicate the concern because imaging, destination, and treatment differ. Avoid delay from extensive office testing.

Part 13 — Pulmonary Embolism

Consider PE with unexplained dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia, syncope, hemoptysis, DVT findings, or right-heart strain, especially with surgery, immobility, cancer, estrogen exposure, pregnancy/postpartum status, or prior VTE.

Prediction tools and D-dimer apply only to validated populations and probability ranges. Instability, syncope with compromise, severe hypoxemia, or high clinical risk requires emergency care, not outpatient rule-out testing.

Part 14 — Acute Dyspnea

Differentiate airway obstruction, asthma or COPD, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, PE, pneumothorax, metabolic acidosis, anemia, arrhythmia, neuromuscular failure, and toxic exposure. First determine severity, then mechanism.

Inability to speak, cyanosis, altered state, silent chest, severe retractions, unilateral absent air entry, frothy secretions, exhaustion, or worsening despite therapy requires escalation. Anxiety is considered only after dangerous causes.

Part 15 — Severe Asthma and COPD

Assess prior ICU or intubation, speech, accessory-muscle use, air entry, oxygenation, rate, mental status, trigger, and response. A falling respiratory rate in an exhausted patient or increasing somnolence is ominous.

Begin protocol-based bronchodilator and supportive care within scope while arranging transfer for severe disease. Antibiotics are not automatic for every exacerbation.

Part 16 — Anaphylaxis

Anaphylaxis may involve airway swelling, bronchospasm, hypotension, GI symptoms, or widespread skin findings after a likely trigger; skin findings can be absent. Intramuscular epinephrine is first-line. Antihistamines and corticosteroids do not replace or delay it.

Activate EMS, support airway and circulation, position according to physiology, repeat assessment, and follow current protocol. Observation and follow-up depend on severity, response, comorbidity, and recurrence risk.

Part 17 — Shock Mechanisms

  • Hypovolemic: blood or fluid loss reduces preload.
  • Cardiogenic: pump failure reduces forward flow and may cause congestion.
  • Distributive: vasodilation and maldistributed flow occur in sepsis or anaphylaxis.
  • Obstructive: PE, tamponade, or tension pneumothorax blocks circulation.

Mixed shock is common. Recognize the likely mechanism while stabilizing because a treatment helpful for one type can harm another.

Part 18 — Sepsis

Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated response to infection and is a medical emergency. Suspect it when infection is possible and altered mental status, hypotension, tachypnea, hypoxemia, oliguria, mottling, severe weakness, or other organ dysfunction occurs.

Begin current protocol-based evaluation and treatment without waiting for fever or leukocytosis. Very young, older, pregnant/postpartum, or immunocompromised patients may present atypically. Source control and destination capability matter.

Part 19 — Stroke and TIA

Sudden facial weakness, arm weakness, speech change, visual loss, severe imbalance, neglect, or another focal deficit is a stroke emergency. Determine exact last known well, glucose, anticoagulant use, recent surgery or bleeding, baseline function, and evolution.

Activate EMS to a stroke-capable system. Do not delay for outpatient imaging or drive the patient privately. A resolved deficit may be TIA and still requires urgent evaluation.

Part 20 — Headache Emergencies

Red flags include thunderclap onset, focal deficit, altered consciousness, seizure, papilledema, fever with meningismus, pregnancy/postpartum state, cancer, immune compromise, new age-associated pattern, significant trauma, or progression.

A migraine history does not eliminate risk when the episode differs. Sudden maximal pain may represent subarachnoid hemorrhage or vascular disease; emergency imaging strategy depends on timing and context.

Part 21 — Seizure

During active seizure, protect from injury, manage airway and breathing, check glucose, time the event, and follow current emergency protocol. Do not place objects in the mouth. Prolonged or recurrent seizure without recovery requires emergency treatment and transport.

Afterward assess return to baseline, focal findings, fever, pregnancy, medication adherence, poison, trauma, electrolytes, withdrawal, and prior history. Persistent altered state is not assumed to be routine postictal recovery.

Part 22 — Hypoglycemia

Symptoms include sweating, tremor, hunger, palpitations, behavior change, confusion, seizure, or coma. Check glucose promptly in altered mental status and treat according to consciousness, swallowing safety, access, and protocol.

Identify insulin or secretagogue exposure, reduced intake, kidney dysfunction, alcohol, sepsis, liver disease, or dosing error. Long-acting medication effects may require observation after initial correction.

Part 23 — DKA and Hyperglycemic Crisis

Polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, dehydration, vomiting, abdominal pain, deep breathing, altered state, or marked hyperglycemia suggests DKA or another hyperglycemic emergency. Confirm glucose, ketones, electrolytes, and acid-base status in an appropriate setting.

Fluid, insulin, and electrolyte management requires protocol-based monitoring. Serum potassium can be normal or high despite total-body depletion. Do not give a casual outpatient correction to a vomiting, dehydrated, or ketotic patient.

Part 24 — Electrolyte and Renal Emergencies

Severe hyperkalemia can cause fatal arrhythmia; severe sodium disturbance can cause seizure and brain dysfunction. AKI may cause volume overload, acidosis, uremic symptoms, and medication accumulation.

Interpret critical results with symptoms, ECG, sample quality, renal function, drugs, and trend. Immediate patient contact and escalation are required; an unconfirmed voicemail is not closed-loop care.

Part 25 — GI Bleeding

Assess hematemesis, melena, hematochezia, anticoagulants, liver disease, NSAIDs, syncope, pain, and hemodynamics. Hematochezia can reflect brisk upper bleeding. Early hemoglobin and normal blood pressure do not exclude major acute loss.

Altered state, syncope, active bleeding, orthostatic compromise, tachycardia, severe anemia, or significant comorbidity requires emergency evaluation. Communicate antithrombotic exposure.

Part 26 — Acute Abdominal and Pelvic Threats

Consider perforation, obstruction, appendicitis, ischemia, aneurysm, pancreatitis, biliary infection, ectopic pregnancy, and ovarian or testicular torsion. Peritonitis, pulsatile mass, bilious emesis, bleeding, shock, pain out of proportion, rigid abdomen, or rapid progression are red flags.

Pregnancy status can alter the differential and imaging plan, but stabilization should not wait. Sudden testicular or unilateral pelvic pain requires time-sensitive torsion assessment.

Part 27 — Pregnancy and Postpartum Emergencies

Hemodynamic instability, severe bleeding, ectopic-pregnancy pattern, severe hypertension with neurologic or epigastric symptoms, seizure, chest pain, dyspnea, fever, or postpartum deterioration requires obstetric-capable emergency care.

Pregnancy changes physiology, medication risk, imaging decisions, and destination needs. Postpartum risk does not end at hospital discharge; hemorrhage, hypertension, infection, cardiomyopathy, VTE, and psychiatric emergency can appear later.

Part 28 — Poisoning and Overdose

Assess airway, breathing, circulation, glucose, temperature, pupils, skin, bowel sounds, mental status, ECG when indicated, substance, dose, time, route, co-exposures, intent, and container. Do not induce vomiting or give a home antidote without expert direction.

In the United States, Poison Control provides expert guidance at 1-800-222-1222 or through webPOISONCONTROL. Call emergency services first for collapse, seizure, respiratory difficulty, severe symptoms, or immediate danger.

Part 29 — Opioid Toxicity

Respiratory depression and reduced consciousness are the central threats. Support ventilation, activate EMS, and administer naloxone according to current training and protocol when opioid toxicity is suspected. Naloxone does not replace airway and breathing support.

Response may be temporary, and potent or long-acting exposures may recur. After survival, address overdose risk, naloxone access, substance-use treatment, medication for opioid use disorder, and respectful follow-up.

Part 30 — Trauma and Head Injury

Identify airway or cervical concerns, breathing asymmetry, hemorrhage, neurologic change, mechanism, anticoagulants, intoxication, and distracting injury. A low-height fall can be serious in an older adult or anticoagulated patient.

Clinical decision rules apply only to validated populations and do not override instability, focal deficits, suspected abuse, or clinician concern. Worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizure, confusion, weakness, or declining consciousness requires urgent evaluation.

Part 31 — Behavioral Emergency

Assess medical stability before psychiatric attribution. Evaluate suicide or violence risk, intent, plan, means, psychosis, mania, intoxication, withdrawal, delirium, capacity, abuse, and ability to care for self.

Imminent danger, severe agitation with medical compromise, catatonia, overdose, dangerous withdrawal, or inability to maintain safety requires emergency crisis care. Use calm, trauma-informed de-escalation and the least restrictive safe approach. In the United States, 988 supports crisis response; immediate life-threatening danger requires emergency services.

Part 32 — Telehealth Emergency Recognition

Confirm the patient’s exact location, callback number, identity, and who is present early when acuity is possible. Observe speech, breathing, color, movement, and cognition, but acknowledge the limits of remote vital signs and examination.

If emergency evaluation is needed, keep the patient connected when feasible, activate local emergency resources, discourage driving, enlist a safe nearby person, and transmit relevant information. A video connection does not make an unstable patient safe at home.

Part 33 — EMS Transport and Handoff

Private transport is unsafe when deterioration, cardiac arrest, airway compromise, severe bleeding, neurologic progression, altered consciousness, or need for monitoring is possible. EMS can treat en route and communicate with the receiving system.

Use a concise handoff: patient and baseline; exact onset or last known well; primary concern; vital trends; key examination; medications such as anticoagulants or insulin; allergies; pregnancy; interventions and response; and remaining uncertainty. Send relevant records without delaying transport.

Part 34 — Board-Style Case 1: Normal ECG, Ongoing Risk

A 62-year-old with diabetes has pressure, diaphoresis, nausea, and dyspnea. The first office ECG is nondiagnostic. The correct action is EMS transfer for ACS evaluation—not antacid treatment and a routine appointment.

Reasoning chain: ischemic symptom cluster + high-risk context → one normal tracing cannot exclude ACS → serial emergency evaluation is required.

Part 35 — Board-Style Case 2: Rash Without Hives

Minutes after an injection, a patient develops throat tightness, wheeze, vomiting, and hypotension without hives. This still meets a high-risk anaphylaxis pattern.

Reasoning chain: likely trigger + airway/breathing/circulatory involvement → intramuscular epinephrine first → EMS, supportive care, and reassessment.

Part 36 — Board-Style Case 3: Resolved Weakness

A patient had unilateral weakness and aphasia for 15 minutes and is now normal. Symptom resolution does not make routine follow-up safe.

Reasoning chain: sudden focal deficit → possible TIA or stroke → urgent stroke-system assessment and secondary-risk evaluation.

Part 37 — Board-Style Case 4: “Anxiety”

A postpartum patient with sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, and presyncope is labeled anxious. Pregnancy-associated VTE risk and the symptom pattern demand emergency PE evaluation.

Reasoning chain: high-risk state + cardiopulmonary symptoms → exclude life threat before psychiatric attribution.

Part 38 — Board-Style Case 5: Critical Result

A laboratory reports potassium 6.8 mEq/L in a patient with CKD who now feels weak. Leaving a message is insufficient. Contact the patient directly, assess symptoms and medication risks, and arrange immediate emergency evaluation.

Reasoning chain: critical electrolyte + arrhythmia risk → closed-loop contact and urgent ECG-capable care.

Part 39 — Common Board Traps

  • Trap: Normal blood pressure means stable.
    Correction: compensated shock and other emergencies may precede hypotension.
  • Trap: A normal initial ECG excludes ACS.
    Correction: integrate risk, symptoms, serial testing, and trajectory.
  • Trap: No hives means no anaphylaxis.
    Correction: skin findings may be absent; epinephrine treats the emergency.
  • Trap: Resolved deficit can wait.
    Correction: TIA can precede stroke and needs urgent evaluation.
  • Trap: Quiet breathing means improvement.
    Correction: silent chest or fatigue can signal respiratory failure.
  • Trap: A diagnosis must be complete before EMS is called.
    Correction: identify failing physiology and activate resources early.
  • Trap: Private transport is always faster.
    Correction: high-risk patients need monitoring, treatment, and destination coordination.
  • Trap: Sending the patient ends responsibility.
    Correction: document, hand off, own pending results, and arrange post-event follow-up.

Part 40 — Final Board-Ready Algorithm

  1. Look: identify abnormal appearance, breathing, color, behavior, bleeding, or collapse.
  2. Activate: call emergency resources early when instability is possible.
  3. Assess ABCDE: stabilize immediate threats within scope and training.
  4. Check rapid reversibles: glucose, oxygenation, exposure, hemorrhage, temperature, and medications.
  5. Name time-critical diagnoses: connect each to required intervention and destination.
  6. Reassess: trend symptoms, vital signs, mental status, and response.
  7. Transport safely: use EMS and appropriate specialty destination when deterioration is possible.
  8. Handoff clearly: onset, baseline, concern, trends, treatment, response, risks, and uncertainty.
  9. Close the loop: records, pending results, family communication, reconciliation, and follow-up.

High-Yield Summary

  • Emergency care begins with physiology and ABCDE, not diagnostic perfection.
  • Instability includes airway, respiratory, perfusion, neurologic, hemorrhagic, toxicologic, and behavioral threats—not hypotension alone.
  • Normal initial ECG, saturation, blood pressure, or temporary improvement can create false reassurance.
  • Sepsis, stroke, ACS, anaphylaxis, respiratory failure, shock, metabolic crisis, overdose, and pregnancy emergencies are time-sensitive.
  • Intramuscular epinephrine is first-line for anaphylaxis; antihistamines do not replace it.
  • Altered mental status requires glucose and a medical/toxic differential before psychiatric labeling.
  • Testing should not delay EMS or definitive treatment when the setting cannot safely complete care.
  • High-risk patients should not drive or travel unmonitored by private vehicle.
  • A structured handoff transmits baseline, onset, trends, interventions, response, risks, and uncertainty.
  • Disposition is incomplete until transfer, documentation, pending-result ownership, and follow-up are closed.

Evidence Anchors

  • American Heart Association: 2025 CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care guidelines.
  • CDC: sepsis is a medical emergency requiring immediate evaluation and treatment.
  • American Stroke Association: current stroke warning signs and emergency response.
  • American College of Emergency Physicians: clinical policy resources for adult mild traumatic brain injury.
  • Poison Control: 24/7 U.S. exposure guidance at 1-800-222-1222 and webPOISONCONTROL.
  • CMS: emergency screening, stabilizing treatment, and appropriate transfer principles under EMTALA for covered hospital emergency departments.

Clinical note: This lesson is educational and does not replace certified resuscitation training, local protocol, medical direction, or patient-specific emergency assessment. Apply current AHA, CDC, ACEP, stroke-system, poison-center, obstetric, trauma, behavioral-crisis, EMS, scope-of-practice, and facility procedures. Activate emergency services for immediate life-threatening danger.
